'''''Actinidia chinensis''''' is a fruiting vine native to [[China]]. It is one of some 40 related species of the [[genus]] ''[[Actinidia]]'', and the origin of most commercial varieties of [[kiwifruit]].

There are three accepted varieties of the species. [[Actinidia chinensis var. deliciosa|''Actinidia chinensis'' var. ''deliciosa'']], a form which grows primarily in southwestern China that has hairier fruit, was brought to [[New Zealand]] in 1904. Varieties which were developed from these plants are the origin of the major green kiwifruit varieties. ''Actinidia chinensis'' var. ''chinensis'' is a variety which has smoother skin, and typically grows in southeastern China. Fruit from this variety were developed into [[gold kiwifruit]] and [[red kiwifruit]] cultivar in the late 20th and early 21st century, including [[Zespri]] Gold, Zespri SunGold, Jintao, Hongyang and Donghong. The third variety, [[Actinidia chinensis var. setosa|''Actinidia chinensis'' var. ''setosa'']], grows exclusively in Taiwan.

==Taxonomy==

The taxon was first formally described in 1857 by French botanist [[Jules Émile Planchon]],<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/2926277 |title=Sur la nouvelle famille des Cochlospermées |language=French |first1=J. E. |last1=Planchon |author-link1=Jules Émile Planchon |journal=The London Journal of Botany |volume=6 |year=1847 |page=303}}</ref> who used plants collected by [[Robert Fortune]], who was sent to China by the [[Royal Horticultural Society|Horticultural Society of London]] to collect plants in the aftermath of the [[First Opium War]]. Fortune's specimen was likely collected around the year 1845.<ref name="Nomenclature">{{cite book|first1=A. R.|last1=Ferguson|author-link1=Ross Ferguson|chapter=Botanical Nomenclature: ''Actinidia chinensis'', ''Actinidia deliciosa'', and ''Actinidia setosa''|pages=36–57|title=Kiwifruit Science and Management |editor-last1=Warrington |editor-first1=I. J.|editor-last2=Weston|editor-first2=G. C. |year=1990 |location=Auckland |publisher=New Zealand Society for Horticultural Science |isbn=0-908596-28-6}}</ref>{{rp|37-38}} The [[type specimen]] is held at the [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]].<ref name="Nomenclature"/>{{rp|37-38}}

The first recognised variety of ''Actinidia chinensis'' was [[Actinidia chinensis var. deliciosa|''Actinidia chinensis'' var. ''deliciosa'']], described in 1940 by [[Auguste Chevalier]]. Chevalier originally considered the variety to be a type of ''[[Actinidia latifolia]]'', but revised this to ''Actinidia chinensis'' in 1941.<ref name="Chevalier1941">{{citeQ|Q96002308}}</ref><ref name="Botanical">{{cite Q|Q133873315}}</ref> The second, ''[[Actinidia chinensis var. setosa|Actinidia chinensis ''var.'' setosa]]'', or the Taiwanese kiwifruit, was identified in 1952 by [[Hui-lin Li]].<ref name="Original">{{cite Q|Q100559822}}</ref> Other varieties have been proposed which have since been synonymised with ''Actinidia chinensis'' var.''chinensis'', including ''Actinidia chinensis'' var.'' jinggangshanensis'', ''Actinidia chinensis'' var.'' lageniformis'', ''Actinidia chinensis'' var.'' latifolia'', ''Actinidia chinensis'' var.'' nephrocarpa'', ''Actinidia chinensis'' var.'' rufopulpa'' and ''Actinidia multipetaloides''.<ref name="POWO_77227045-1">{{cite POWO |id=77227045-1 |title=''Actinidia chinensis'' var. ''chinensis'' |access-date=24 April 2025}}</ref>

Phylogenetic analysis has shown that ''Actinidia chinensis ''var.'' setosa'' and ''Actinidia chinensis ''var. ''deliciosa'' are more closely related to each other than to ''Actinidia chinensis ''var.'' chinensis''.<ref>{{cite Q|Q104579682}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Kiwifruit 'Gold' cross section.jpg|thumb|left|Cross-section of a [[gold kiwifruit]] ]]

''Actinidia chinensis'' has a smooth, bronze skin, with a beak shape at the stem attachment. Flesh colour varies from bright green to a clear, intense yellow.<ref name=ferguson/> This species is sweeter and more aromatic in flavour compared to ''A. deliciosa'', similar to some subtropical fruits.<ref name=ferguson/> One of the most attractive varieties has a red 'iris' around the centre of the fruit and yellow flesh outside.<ref name=zespri/> The yellow fruit obtains a higher market price and, being less hairy than the fuzzy kiwifruit, is more palatable for consumption without peeling.<ref name=ferguson/><ref name=zespri/> A commercially viable variety of this red-ringed kiwifruit, patented as ''EnzaRed'', is a cultivar of the Chinese hong yang variety.<ref name="jones">{{cite web |first=Matthew |last=Jones |title=EnzaRed reaches commercial volumes |url=http://www.fruitnet.com/asiafruit/article/160968/enzared-reaches-commercial-volumes |publisher=Fruitnet.com, Market Intelligence Ltd |accessdate=26 May 2019 |date=18 March 2014}}</ref> Fruit colour may vary from green to [[lime (fruit)|lime green]] or gold, depending on [[plant breeding|breeding]].<ref name=ferguson>{{cite web|last=Ferguson|first=Allan Ross|date=1999|publisher=ASHS Press; Purdue University |location=Alexandria, Virginia|pages=342–347|title=New Temperate Fruits: ''Actinidia chinensis'' and ''Actinidia deliciosa''; In: Perspectives on new crops and new uses, J. Janick (ed.)|url=https://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/proceedings1999/v4-342.html}}</ref>

'Hort16A' is a golden kiwifruit cultivar marketed worldwide as Zespri Gold,<ref name=ferguson/> This cultivar suffered significant losses in New Zealand from late 2010 to 2013 due to the [[Pseudomonas syringae|PSA bacterium]]. A new cultivar of golden kiwifruit, 'Zesy002', was found to be more disease-resistant and most growers changed to this cultivar, with its worldwide demand continuing into 2019.<ref name="newshub">{{cite news |first=Angie |last=Skerrett |title=Zespri reports record revenue, as global kiwifruit sales boom |url=https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/rural/2019/05/zespi-reports-record-revenue-as-global-kiwifruit-sales-boom.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190523053250/https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/rural/2019/05/zespi-reports-record-revenue-as-global-kiwifruit-sales-boom.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=May 23, 2019 |accessdate=26 May 2019 |work=New Zealand NewsHub |date=23 May 2019}}</ref> This cultivar is marketed as Zespri SunGold.<ref name="zespri">{{cite web |title=Zespri SunGold kiwifruit |url=https://www.zespri.eu/en/sungold-kiwi |publisher=Zespri Group Ltd. |accessdate=26 May 2019 |date=2019}}</ref> 

==Habitat==
In its native habitat, ''Actinidia chinensis'' grows in thickets, thick ([[oak]]) forests (e.g. ''Quercus aquifolioides'', ''Quercus oxyodon'', ''[[Quercus lamellosa]]''), and light secondary forests and bushland. ''A. chinensis'' prefers slopes and likes also to grow in [[ravine]]s, top heights of {{cvt|200|–|230|m}}, relative to the local [[microclimate]]. In Western gardens it may range {{cvt|30|ft|-1|order=flip}} in all directions, making it unsuitable for all but the largest spaces unless pruned back hard at the end of every growing season.{{citation needed|date=April 2021}}

==Range==

''Actinidia chinensis'' is found in southern China and Taiwan. ''Actinidia chinensis'' var. ''deliciosa'' grows in inland forested areas of southwestern [[China]], while ''Actinidia chinensis'' var. ''chinensis'' typically grows in warmer coastal provinces of southeastern China.<ref name="Nomenclature"/>{{rp|49-51}} The two varieties have overlapping ranges in southeastern [[Shaanxi]], southwestern [[Henan]], western [[Hubei]] and [[Hunan]], where intermediate forms can be found.<ref name="Nomenclature"/>{{rp|49-51}} ''Actinidia chinensis'' var. ''setosa'' is endemic to Taiwan.<ref name="Nomenclature"/>{{rp|49-51}}

==Varieties==
Three varieties are accepted.<ref name = powo/>
*''Actinidia chinensis'' var. ''chinensis'' – central and southern China
*[[Actinidia chinensis var. deliciosa|''Actinidia chinensis'' var. ''deliciosa'']] {{small|(A.Chev.) A.Chev.}} – central and southern China
*[[Actinidia chinensis var. setosa|''Actinidia chinensis'' var. ''setosa'']] {{small|H.L.Li}} – Taiwan

==History==
[[File:Actinidia chinensis 247847581.jpg|thumb|Wild ''Actinidia chinensis'' growing in [[Zhejiang]] Province]]

{{Main|Gold kiwi}}

Traditional Chinese names for the fruit include míhóutáo ({{lang-zh|c=獼猴桃|tr=macaque peach}}), húlítáo ({{lang-zh|c=狐狸桃|tr=fox peach}}), ténglí ({{lang-zh|c=藤梨|tr=vine pear}}) and yángtáo ({{lang-zh|c=羊桃|tr=sheep peach}}),<ref name="Kiwifruit2023">{{cite Q|Q133308627}}</ref><ref name="TamarilloKiwifruit2020">{{cite Q|Q133513057}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| volume = 7| issue = 1| pages = 1–6| last1 = 徐宏化| last2 = 魏芳| last3 = 杨娜| last4 = 赵佳| last5 = 杨嘉辉| last6 = 吕素华| title = 奇异水果猕猴桃--起源, 栽培和应用| journal = Horticulture| date = 2017}}</ref> however no traditional distinction existed between ''Actinidia chinensis'' and ''Actinidia deliciosa'', with míhóutáo and yángtáo being names used to refer to both varieties.<ref name="Kiwifruit2023"/><ref name="Nomenclature">{{cite book|first1=A. R.|last1=Ferguson|author-link1=Ross Ferguson|chapter=Botanical Nomenclature: ''Actinidia chinensis'', ''Actinidia deliciosa'', and ''Actinidia setosa''|pages=36–57|title=Kiwifruit Science and Management |editor-last1=Warrington |editor-first1=I. J.|editor-last2=Weston|editor-first2=G. C. |year=1990 |location=Auckland |publisher=New Zealand Society for Horticultural Science |isbn=0-908596-28-6}}</ref>{{rp|40}} The first known references to ''Actinidia'' plants in China date to the [[Tang dynasty]] in the 800s, when sporadic attempts were made to cultivate the fruit.<ref name="Kiwifruit2023"/><ref>{{cite book|title=Actinidia in China |last1=Cui |first1=Zhixue |last2=Huang |first2=Hongwen |last3=Xiao |first3=Xingguo |date=January 2002 |publisher=China Agricultural and Technology Press |isbn=7801673425}}</ref> This includes a Tang Dynasty poem written by [[Cen Shen]], set in [[Shaanxi]], which describes a plant growing above a well; suggesting that the plant may have been cultivated in gardens during this period.<ref>{{cite book|first1=A. R.|last1=Ferguson|author-link1=Ross Ferguson|chapter=The Kiwifruit in China|pages=157|title=Kiwifruit Science and Management |editor-last1=Warrington |editor-first1=I. J.|editor-last2=Weston|editor-first2=G. C. |year=1990 |location=Auckland |publisher=New Zealand Society for Horticultural Science |isbn=0-908596-28-6}}</ref> In the ''Běncǎo Yǎnyì'' ({{lang-zh|c=本草衍義}}), a 12th century medicinal compendium by Kou Zongshi, describes the plant as growing along pathways deep in the mountains of China, and notes that monkeys eat the fruit.<ref name="Kiwifruit2023"/> Míhóutáo, including ''Actinidia deliciosa'', were traditionally seen as a wild plant, and were often collected and sold at markets in central Chinese provinces.<ref name="Kiwifruit2023"/>

The first European botanist to see a specimen of the plant was [[Pierre Nicolas d'Incarville]], who visited the Imperial Court at [[Beijing]] between 1740 and 1757. One of the specimens that d'Incarville sent back to Paris was of a yang-tao collected from [[Macao]], however these specimens were not described when they reached Paris, and only analysed almost 150 years later.<ref name="Nomenclature"/>{{rp|37-38}} [[Charles Maries]], collecting for [[Veitch Nurseries|Messrs Veitch]] noted it in [[Japan]], but the introduction to Western horticulture was from [[E.H. Wilson]], who sent seeds collected in [[Hubei]] to Veitch in 1900.<ref name=coats>{{cite book|last=Coats|first=Alice M.|chapter=Actinidia|title=Garden Shrubs and Their History|others=Foreword by John L. Creech|orig-year=1964|year=1992|location=New York|publisher=Simon & Schuster|isbn=0-671-74733-9|pages=13–14|url=https://archive.org/details/gardenshrubsthei0000coat/page/n7/mode/2up|access-date=16 January 2025|via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref>

Cultivation of ''Actinidia chinensis'' var. ''deliciosa'' began in [[New Zealand]] in the early 20th century after [[Mary Isabel Fraser]], the principal of [[Whanganui Girls' College]], brought seeds of the plant back to New Zealand.<ref name="Kiwifruit2023"/><ref>{{cite web|title=Isabel Fraser: Hand carried the first kiwifruit seeds from China |url=http://zesprikiwi.com/about/history/isabel-fraser |publisher=Zespri |accessdate=4 January 2013 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120912030603/http://zesprikiwi.com/about/history/isabel-fraser |archivedate=12 September 2012 }}</ref><ref name="Hayward">{{cite web|url=http://php.truelogic.com.ar/zespri/about/history/hayward-wright|publisher=Zespri|title=Hayward Kiwifruits Namesake|accessdate=29 November 2012 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://archive.today/20121229222444/http://php.truelogic.com.ar/zespri/about/history/hayward-wright|archivedate=29 December 2012}}</ref> Over time, numerous cultivars were developed by different growers, all originating from the same plant material that was brought to New Zealand by Fraser.<ref name="Kiwifruit2023"/> By the 1950s, the fruit began to be exported overseas, and by 1959 the name [[kiwifruit]] was adopted.<ref name="TeArapg2">{{cite web|url=https://teara.govt.nz/en/kiwifruit/page-2 |title=Kiwifruit - Early history, names and varieties |first1=Hugh |last1=Campbell |first2=Julia |last2=Haggerty |website=[[Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand]] |date=24 November 2008 |access-date=27 March 2025}}</ref>

In 1957, the [[China National Botanical Garden]] sourced wild ''Actinidia chinensis'' var. ''deliciosa'' seeds from the [[Qinling]] mountains of [[Shaanxi]], growing the first specimens in a botanical institute in China.<ref name="Kiwifruit2023"/> By 1974, Chinese horticulturists began surveying wild [[germplasm]] of ''Actinidia'' species growing in mountainous central China, looking to develop cultivars which could compete with the popularity of New Zealand kiwifruit cultivars.<ref name="Kiwifruit2023"/><ref name="Huang">{{Cite journal| issn = 0018-5345| volume = 37| issue = 7| pages = 1135–1136| last1 = Huang| first1 = Hongwen| last2 = Wang| first2 = Shengmei| last3 = Huang| first3 = Renhuang| last4 = Jiang| first4 = Zhengwang| last5 = Zhang| first5 = Zhonghui| title = 'Jintao', a novel, hairless, yellow-fleshed kiwifruit| journal = HortScience| date = 2002| doi = 10.21273/HORTSCI.37.7.1135| doi-access = free}}</ref> These surveys revealed the potential for golden and red ''Actinidia chinensis'' var. ''chinensis'' varieties to become cultivated commercial crops.<ref name="Kiwifruit2023"/> In the late 1990s, New Zealand kiwifruit exporters [[Zespri]] began to market a [[gold kiwifruit]] cultivar grown from ''Actinidia chinensis'' var. ''chinensis''.<ref name="Kiwifruit2023"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ferguson |first=A.R. |date=1999 |editor-last=Janick |editor-first=J. |title=New temperate fruits: Actinidia chinensis and Actinidia deliciosa |url=https://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/proceedings1999/v4-342.html |journal=Perspectives on New Crops and New Uses |publisher=ASHS Press |publication-place=[[Alexandria, Virginia|Alexandria, VA]] |pages=342–347}}</ref>
